Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Vignette:
Talia was forty-three when the pulmonary embolism nearly killed her. She had been on tour, sleeping on a tour bus, feeling a strange tightness in her chest that she attributed to exhaustion and the dry air of the Midwest. By the time she gasped awake in a Kansas City emergency room, a doctor was telling her that a clot had travelled from her leg and lodged in her lung. She remembered the oxygen mask, the cold stethoscope on her sternum, and the terrifying, hollow sensation of trying to draw a breath that would not come. That moment—the sheer, panicked struggle for air—had lodged itself in her body like a splinter she could not remove.

Three years later, Talia was still a working musician, but her life had narrowed dramatically. She was a guitarist and vocalist for a folk-rock trio, and her bandmates had grown accustomed to her strange new habits. She no longer travelled. She had told them she was done with the road, and they had accepted it, but they did not understand why. The truth was that she could not bear to be more than ten minutes from a major hospital. She had mapped the safe zone of her city with obsessive precision: her home, the studio where they rehearsed, and one café two blocks from the hospital. Anywhere else, her body began to react before her mind caught up. She would be standing in a grocery store, reaching for a carton of milk, and suddenly her heart would hammer, her throat would close, and she would be back in that Kansas City bed, fighting for air. There was no thought involved—just a raw, physical alarm that seized her without warning.

The smells were the worst. A whiff of antiseptic from a public restroom, the faint chemical scent of a cleaning product, even the particular odour of a hotel lobby—all of it could trigger the same suffocating panic. She had learned to avoid hospitals altogether, skipping her annual physical and telling her husband she was too busy for a check-up. The idea of lying on an examination table, with a doctor leaning over her, made her feel as though the clot were already reforming in her lungs. She knew it was irrational, but she could not trust herself. She had come to believe that her own body was a betrayer, and that her reactions since the event—the hypervigilance, the avoidance, the way she woke at three in the morning to check her pulse and listen to her own breathing—proved that she was a lousy coper. Other people survived medical emergencies and moved on. She had collapsed into a life of constant vigilance.

Her marriage had become strained. Her husband, a gentle man who worked in construction, tried to be patient, but he did not understand why she would not go to dinner downtown, or why she flinched when he coughed. She had started to tell herself that she deserved this suffering—that she had ignored her body for years, pushing through tours and late nights, and that the clot was a punishment for her own neglect. This thought looped through her mind during the quiet hours of the night, when she lay awake, listening to the sound of her own lungs expanding and contracting, waiting for the next catastrophe. She would think about how different her life would have been if she had never gotten on that tour bus, if she had stayed home, if she had listened to the first twinge of pain. The counterfactuals played like a broken record, each one a reminder of her own inadequacy.

What finally brought her to seek help was a single, ordinary moment. She was in the studio, tuning her guitar, when she smelled hand sanitizer on her bandmate’s hands. Her chest seized, her vision blurred, and she had to sit down on the floor, gasping, while her bandmate stared at her in alarm. That night, her husband told her, gently, that he could not keep watching her shrink. She came to therapy because she was exhausted, and because she was afraid that if she did not change, she would lose the life she had built. She hoped, more than anything, to feel safe in her own skin again—but she was terrified that she never would.
